blocks.p: Once you can anchor into safety and [Validate and Normalize](piece:validating-and-normalizing) what you feel, it's time for the next skill: Balancing. Balancing is your ability to mindfully anchor in safety, allow a defensive experience, and then intentionally shift your focus back to safety, allowing both safety and defense to be present within you at the same time.
Balancing takes welcoming defense a step further by actively feeling it, even if just a little bit. Start with mild defensive activation.

Balancing is Active self-regulation, requiring deliberate effort and intention as you connect with defense and safety. It also helps transitioning into Received self-regulation. Your ability to stay grounded in safety and use that grounding to support defense is vital for what comes next.

As you practice Balancing, you will notice several benefits. In the short term, successful Balancing can soften defense. But in the long term, repeated Balancing practices can reduce your daily chronic defensive activation. Over time, distress tolerance can increase and you are better capable of regulating through distress.

Balancing activates safety, deactivates it, and then reactivates it again. This cycle of removing and re-engaging the safety state is what Dr. Porges calls a "neural exercise." Neural exercises directly strengthen the ventral vagal pathways.
"Isn't that a good thing, Justin?"
Yer darn right it is.

Besides the short-term benefit of softening your defense and the long-term gain of higher distress tolerance, Balancing can also boost your confidence. Each time you successfully experience a defensive response and then recover in safety, you build confidence. You realize you can manage these internal experiences. This increases your belief that you can not only succeed but also do it again, even at deeper levels or for longer periods of time. You'll find that leaning into defense isn't as scary as you once thought, eventually leading you to welcome those internal experiences you once avoided.
You can use Balancing both reactively and proactively. Of course, I highly recommend practicing proactively.

Reactively, use Balancing to soften a defensive reaction that has been triggered, like when your spouse doesn't put their socks into the hamper. (Or something more serious, but start light.) Reactive Balancing responds to uninvited emotions (like annoyance at the socks). Notice the defense and intentionally allow it to remain, then shift your focus toward safety.

Reactive Balancing requires a high level of internal awareness and a fairly strong vagal brake. I recommend using reactive Balancing for mild to moderate defensive emotions, such as irritation at another driver, frustration when your kids won't go to bed, or a tolerable Obstacle that surfaces during meditation.

Proactively use Balancing to intentionally practice feeling defense that you know is chronic within you. This proactive practice can help reduce the intensity of that defensive emotion, strengthen your vagal brake, and lower the persistent level of that emotion in your system daily. You could also use proactive Balancing to prepare for future defensive emotions and build tolerance to them, such as the anxiety before an upcoming medical visit.

You'll gain more from Proactive Balancing by carefully noticing and feeling the smallest level of defense and the shortest time your system can handle. As this becomes easier, you can then increase the depth of defense and the duration. For example, you might first Balance an emotion like disappointment before tackling shame. Once disappointment becomes easier, move on to something more challenging, like frustration. As that becomes manageable, keep welcoming more difficult emotions, progressing toward the core defensive feelings you hold inside.

Proactive Balancing includes emotions that you choose, but also the Obstacles that surface as you explore your inner world. As an Obstacle presents itself, use the opportunity to Balance, then decide to stay with it or focus on safety or end your practice.
Let's look at three levels of Balancing through A->W->E.

Balancing at Anchored Awareness is suitable for beginners or those with low tolerance. If this is challenging, you are not required to sit with defense. Focus on [Validating and Normalizing](piece:validating-and-normalizing) first, then Balancing.

To transition into Balancing, try it with Validating and Normalizing first! Validate a defense emotion, then shift to safety. You can then Validate and Normalize, then shift to safety. Listen to your capacity and work within it before diving deeper with Witnessing & Balancing.

When Balancing at the Witness level, you'll briefly engage with the defensive emotion, noticing where it is in the body. If you can mindfully connect with the defense for a moment, then shift your focus to safety, consider it a success.

For clients new to feeling defense, I will guide them through "skipping stones." You know how a smooth, flat stone skips across the water's surface when thrown just right? It's similar with Balancing: you'll lightly skim the surface. So when I say a second of noticing is a win, I mean it! Anchor into safety, lightly skim defense, then return to safety.

blocks.why: Every Balance starts with a firm anchor. This practice is that first anchor.

blocks.p: I'll reiterate: you shouldn't stay in defense longer than is tolerable. If you only skim the surface, that's fine! As skimming becomes easier, spend more time with it and move on to Experiencing Balancing.
If you can maintain safety while Balancing defense in the body, then it's time to Experience it through Description. These basic description questions are usually enough:
Anchor yourself in safety, bring your awareness to a defensive Emotion, find where it resides in the body, describe its Sensation, then redirect your focus back to safety.

If Balancing is easy for you at all three levels of A->W->E, then it's time to move on to the next Skill. However, you can also increase the challenge by practicing outside your Passive Safety Environment before progressing. I highly recommend practicing both inside and outside this space before moving to the next Skill.
"I can't shift my focus back to safety once I'm in defense."

This means you went too deep into defense or your safety anchoring wasn't strong enough to start. For your next practice: (1) Anchor more firmly in safety before turning to defense. (2) Touch defense even more lightly.
"I Balance once, and the defense completely disappears."
This can happen, especially with milder defense. Notice what replaces it and use the Skills you have as needed.
"When I shift to safety, nothing happens. The defense remains at the same intensity."

Balancing doesn't always lead to immediate softening: especially early in practice. The key is shifting your focus and staying anchored in safety, even as the defense continues. This process builds capacity. Over time and with repeated practice, you'll notice the defense softening more consistently. For now, just practicing the shift is enough.
"I don't know which depth level to practice."

Start with Anchored Awareness by Validating and Normalizing defense. Practice that for several sessions until it feels easy. Then move on to Witnessing and observe where defense resides for 1-2 seconds. Only progress to Experiencing when Witnessing feels comfortable, and you're genuinely curious to explore more.
"Balancing feels boring or pointless."
Building capacity happens through small, repeated actions. Think of it like lifting weights. One rep doesn't do much, but 100 reps over the course of weeks build strength.
Balancing is the ability to consciously anchor into safety, allow a defensive experience, and intentionally shift focus back to safety. It's Active Self-Regulation that increases capacity.

When beginning to Balance, start with Anchored Awareness (using the Cognitive Openers), then move to Witnessing (noticing where defense resides, even for 1-2 seconds, using "skipping stones"), and advance to Experiencing (describing) only when Witnessing feels easy.

Use Balancing both reactively (to soften existing defense) and proactively (for planned practice), always prioritizing safety anchoring. Stopping to re-anchor when needed isn't failure; it's building capacity.

Attempt one Balance - firmly anchor in safety, briefly acknowledge a mild defensive Emotion for one second, then return your focus to safety. If easy, spend longer on defense or use Description. If this feels too hard, spend more time Validating and Normalizing.

Can you continue to practice Balancing regularly?
What level of A->W->E did you practice with?

blocks.p: You've learned how to anchor into safety, Validate, Normalize, and Balance defense with safety. You've carefully entered discomfort and found your way back to solid ground. Now, you're ready to progress with Pendulating.

Pendulating is the ability to deliberately and consciously shift between feelings of safety and defense. It's similar to Balancing, but with Pendulating, you continuously alternate between defense and safety. A Pendulation exercise begins in safety, shifts to defense, returns to safety, shifts again to defense, and ends in safety. This process involves at least two pendulations.

Performing two pendulations is a significant achievement if this skill is new to you. As you gain confidence, add more pendulations as you see fit. Pay attention to what your body can handle without overdoing it. Keep the Interest Impulse in mind as well. As long as you still feel it, it's likely okay to continue pendulating. When curiosity lessens or hesitation appears, it's probably time to stop, unless you can tune into the hesitation. Additionally, the [four signs it's time to stop](piece:starting-and-stopping#when-to-stop) indicate it's time to end.

Otherwise, Pendulate as much or as little as you like; there is no magic number, specific time, or set number of pendulations. When I lead live skills practices, we spend 5-10 minutes anchoring in safety and then work through the Skills Sequence, all the way to two pendulations. As your vagal brake strengthens, you might spend more mindful, compassionate time in defensive activation without becoming dysregulated.

As you know (but I need to repeat), the priority is always to stay sufficiently anchored in your safety state. While much of this work involves feeling your defensive state, you must maintain access to safety. When you shift your focus to defense, it's natural for your safety activation to decrease somewhat. However, it shouldn't decrease so much that you can't pendulate back to your safety experience to consistently balance defense.

Pendulation is very effective for welcoming and guiding sympathetic activation. As you self-regulate out of shutdown, Pendulating can help reintegrate fight activation into your system. Similarly, as you thaw the immobilization of freeze, Pendulating is excellent for guiding and releasing once-frozen sympathetic activation. (The [unstucking methods](piece:unstucking-methods) help release the activation.)

As you successfully Pendulate, you'll notice new layers of stuckness emerging, each peeling back to reveal the next. For example, when you Pendulate anger, you might peel it away only to find hurt. And as you continue Pendulating through that hurt, you could discover rejection. These layers peeling back are nothing new; you've practiced noticing and welcoming them as Obstacles. Keep using the Skills you already have.
You can use Pendulation both reactively and proactively, just like the rest of the Skills Sequence. Of course, I still strongly recommend practicing proactively.

You can pendulate to soften a defensive experience that has already arisen, as long as the intensity is tolerable. Allow the defense, then shift to safety to Balance, and go back and forth as needed. The defensive emotion could be something from the day or an Obstacle that surfaces through meditation.

The above describes Pendulating reactively and is typically more difficult, requiring a strong vagal brake. If you've practiced the preceding skills in the Skills Sequence, your vagal brake has likely strengthened enough to pendulate with mild to moderate defensive emotions, such as irritation and sadness.

You will gain more benefits from practicing Pendulation proactively. Think of Pendulation as a skill you can learn, like any other. You need to practice it to get better. It's not something you will master on your first try. To practice Pendulation proactively, intentionally welcome an easier emotion, then work your way toward more difficult ones. I recommend focusing on daily emotions, like irritation, then gradually challenging yourself with longer-held emotions like shame or guilt.

You can also use Pendulation proactively by intentionally welcoming a likely upcoming emotion, such as anxiety about an upcoming meeting. Focus on the smallest amount of the emotion possible, then gradually increase it as capacity allows.
Let's look at three levels of Pendulating through A->W->E.

Pendulating at Anchored Awareness is best for beginners or those with low distress tolerance. If this is too challenging, focus on Balancing until your distress tolerance increases enough to try Pendulating again.

This level of Pendulating involves Validating and Normalizing the defensive emotion. To build familiarity, you could also Imagine & Invite the defensive experience, then pendulate with it. This is likely easy if you're already Balancing, but it's an option if you want a quick confidence boost.

When Pendulating at the Witness level, briefly acknowledge the defensive emotion and notice where it resides in the body. Consider it a success if you connect with the defense only briefly and pendulate twice. You can also use the "skipping stones" light practice here: anchor into safety, lightly skim the defense, return to safety, lightly skim again (even lighter if needed), and then return to safety once more.

To Pendulate at the Experiencing level, ask descriptive questions and go with whatever comes to mind. You can Describe at any point during your Pendulation practice. I typically guide students and clients through Balancing first, then Pendulate to defense at the Experiencing level. Use these basic questions to Experience defense:

If Pendulating is easy for you at all three levels of A->W->E, it's time to work with more challenging emotions as you explore your inner world. However, you can also increase the challenge by practicing outside your Passive Safety Environment.
"I lose safety anchoring in the first pendulation."
You're trying to Pendulate before you've mastered Balancing. You need to be able to Balance easily and reliably before attempting multiple swings.
"Pendulating makes me more activated, not less."

This can happen if: (1) You're going too deep into defense on each swing (touch it more lightly, "skip stones"), (2) You're doing too many pendulations for your current capacity (try just two pendulations total per session), or (3) Your safety anchoring isn't strong enough. If Pendulating consistently increases activation, return to Balancing. Build more capacity there first.
"The defense doesn't change, no matter how many times I pendulate."

That's okay. The goal isn't to change the defense. The goal is to be with it. You're building capacity and strengthening your vagal brake, not getting rid of the defense. Remember our goal. We want to connect with the present moment, whatever it brings.
"I feel like I'm just going through the motions."

If Pendulation feels mechanical and disconnected, you might be focusing too much on the technique and not enough on the experience. You may also be disconnected. Either way, focus on Experiencing safety first, then try connecting with defense through Balancing.

Pendulation is the ability to intentionally shift repeatedly between safety and defensive activation (not just once, as in Balancing). It is a form of Active Self-Regulation that increases capacity, helps discharge stuck flight/fight energy, and peels back layers of defense.
Begin with two pendulations (safety → defense → safety → defense → safety), practicing at Anchored Awareness, then Witnessing, and then Experiencing, based on your current capacity.
Always prioritize safety anchoring: if you lose access to safety during Pendulation, pause immediately, re-anchor, and return when ready; stopping early builds capacity over time.

Attempt one Pendulation - firmly anchor in safety, briefly acknowledge a mild defensive Emotion for one second, return your focus to safety, then defense, and then safety. If easy, spend longer on defense or use Description. If this feels too hard, spend more time with Balancing.
